1:
Whether Mary Magdalene was a fallen woman is fought out here, and the protest is Clarke's. Commentators have a marvellous propensity, he says, to make the women of the Sacred Writings appear women of ill fame, so that one must be a harlot and this one a prostitute, though nothing of the kind can be proved in either case; she is presented simply as one who had been possessed with seven demons, among other women healed of evil spirits and infirmities, and Joanna and Susanna might as well come in for a share of the censure. He adds a prudential argument: had she been such, the world that knew her character could not see the inward change, and Christ's enemies, who were ready enough to call him the friend of publicans and sinners, would certainly have seized so favourable an opportunity, yet they never said he was the friend of prostitutes. He concludes that the common opinion is a vile slander on one of the best women in the Gospel, and complains that houses for the reception of such bear her name. Barnes says the same more briefly, that it has been commonly supposed but there is not the least evidence for it. Lightfoot, on the other hand, supplies the material the tradition feeds on, reporting a Talmudic Maria Magdila who was an adulteress, and a town near Jerusalem of very ill fame, so that she might be called Magdalene either from living there or from imitating its customs.

On the seven devils they nearly agree, and on the second name they divide again. Barnes and Clarke both take seven for an indefinite number signifying a grievous torment, and Lightfoot says the same, that there is hardly anything more useful than to put a certain number for an uncertain; Ellicott alone gives it a clinical sense, of a specially aggravated possession with paroxysms of delirious frenzy like those of the Gadarene. Lightfoot then derives Chuza from Haman's genealogy and concludes it an Idumean name, fitting for a man in the household of Herod, who was of the blood of the Edomites. Gill contests this on the manuscripts, since in his edition of that treatise Haman's ancestor is not Chuza but Ciza, and Chuza is a Jewish name borne by a family of note, one rabbi being called the Chuzite because he was of that family.

What the women's ministry amounted to they build up between them. Ellicott pictures two travelling companies, the Master and the Twelve heralding his approach in synagogue or market-place or open plain, and a separate company of devout women, mostly of the wealthier class, journeying probably in advance to arrange for his reception and food; he adds that it was said to be no uncommon practice for women of independent means to support a teacher in his work. Tertullian finds the whole arrangement prophesied, applying to these wealthy ladies the summons to the women that are at ease to rise up and hear, so that they were proved first as disciples and then as helpers, following in labour and ministering with hope. Calvin turns their history into an argument about grace, that to be attended by women marked with infamy might be thought dishonourable to the Son of God, but the crimes with which we were loaded before we believed do not diminish his glory, since it is not said that the Church he elected was found without spot but that he cleansed it; they were pointed at with the finger on every side, and willingly endured to have their shame made known provided the grace of Christ were not concealed. Bede describes the method rather than the company, that like the eagle enticing its young to fly, our Lord raises his disciples step by step, teaching first in the synagogues, then choosing the twelve, then taking them with him through the cities and villages.
4:
Why the teaching should be veiled at all is the first question, and Theophylact gives two reasons that pull in opposite directions. The Lord speaks by a parable first that he may make his hearers more attentive, since men were accustomed to exercise their minds on dark sayings and to despise what was plain; and next, that the unworthy might not receive what was spoken mystically. He also finds the method foretold, in the psalm where the promise is to open the mouth in parables. Origen notices the same double effect in the setting: much people were gathered together and were come out of every city, and yet not many but few there are who walk the strait road and find the way that leads to life; hence the other evangelist says that he taught without the house by parables, but within the house explained the parable to his disciples. Henry, who takes no interest in the concealment, dwells on the concourse instead: they came out of every city and would not stay till he came to them, meeting him when he was coming toward them and following him when he was going from them; nor would he excuse himself from going to the cities on that account, for he is found of those that sought him not.

On who the sower is they converge without argument. Gill holds that Christ is chiefly designed, since the phrase his seed, which only this evangelist has, best agrees with him, he being both the proprietor and the subject of it, though it is true of every preacher of the gospel; and he takes the spot chosen for the sowing to be first the people of the Jews and afterwards the Gentiles. Eusebius divides the hearers before the parable divides them, into those who have been made worthy of the heavenly calling but fall from grace through carelessness and sloth, and those who multiply the seed and bear good fruit; he notes that the other evangelist makes three divisions within each class, since those who corrupt the seed have not all the same manner of destruction, and those who bear fruit do not receive an equal abundance. He is also alone in explaining the loss on the wayside without any fault in the hearer, since some, though they have not sinned, have lost the good seed implanted in their hearts through its having been withdrawn from their thoughts and memory by evil spirits, or by deceitful and cunning men, whom he calls the birds of the air.

What is peculiar to this account of the parable the two grammarians pick out, and they agree. Robertson lists what has been added here and nowhere else: his seed, the trampling under foot, the birds of the heavens, and the word for moisture, which occurs in the New Testament only in this verse. Ellicott presses the same words for their sense, preferring upon the rock to the stony or rocky ground of the other two reports, and calling this the more accurate term; and he takes the statement that it withered because it lacked moisture to be obviously not without its force in the spiritual interpretation, the moisture being the dew and rain of God's grace, without which the seed could not put forth its roots. On his reading the two failures on the rock are distinct, since the lack of moisture represents one aspect of what was wanting and the having no depth of earth another. Gill adds the plainer identification, that those who fell upon the rock are hearers whose hearts are hardened through the deceitfulness of sin and continue so notwithstanding the preaching of the word to them.
9:
Whether the parables were meant to hide or only happened to hide is the question the disciples' request forces, and the answers differ in kind. Robertson reports the grammatical difficulty, that one evangelist uses a particle of purpose here where another uses one of cause, and passes on the resolution he thinks sensible, that there is truth in both: Jesus speaks in parables because the multitudes see without seeing and hear without hearing, and also in order that they may. Cyril of Jerusalem reports the objection as a dispute, where one party asks what sort of God causes blindness and the other answers from the apostle that the gospel is veiled only in them that are perishing, since it is not right to give holy things to dogs; and he applies that to this verse, asking whether the Lord wished them not to see from hatred, or because of their unworthiness, since they had closed their own eyes, for where there is wilful wickedness there is also a withholding of grace. Ellicott notes only that the prophet's words are given here without being quoted as such, and Henry turns the whole into a privilege to be felt rather than a problem to be solved: those who would receive instruction from Christ must consider what a distinguishing privilege it is to be led into the light when others are left in darkness, and how happy we are if what is a parable to others, with which they are only amused, is a plain truth to us.

The interpretation itself they handle by noticing what this account adds. Robertson observes that the phrase the word of God, which stands here for the word of the kingdom in the other report, is a favourite of this evangelist and rare elsewhere, and that with the article on both sides the terms are interchangeable, so the word of God is the seed; Ellicott adds that it is to be taken in its widest sense, as including every form by which a revelation from God reaches the mind of man. Both notice that the devil is named here where the others say Satan or the wicked one, and that the purpose given is fuller, lest they should believe and be saved; Robertson makes it the plain reason why preaching fails, the devil's business being to snatch the seed from the heart before it sprouts and takes root. On the rocky hearers Ellicott notes that the trial here is explained by the tribulation or persecution of the other reports, and that falling away stands where the others have being offended.

The good ground is described by two adjectives, and all three of them stop over the phrase. Robertson explains that one word means really good or generous and the other beautiful or noble, that the Greeks joined them to describe the high-minded gentleman, and that the pair occurs here alone in the New Testament, though the evangelist adds moral qualities the pagan phrase did not carry. Ellicott says the same, that the word rendered honest has a higher meaning than the English now bears and is better expressed by noble, and that the two were joined by Greek ethical writers to express the highest ideal of moral excellence. On the last word all three prefer perseverance to patience. Clarke insists on it, since good ground continues to bear because it is strong and vigorous, and poor ground is soon exhausted; from which he draws that the perseverance of the saints necessarily implies continuing to bring forth fruit, and that those who are not fruitful are not in a state of perseverance. Ellicott says the word implies something more vigorous than the passive submission we associate with patience, and Robertson that there is no other way for real fruit to come, since mushrooms spring up overnight but the best fruits require time and cultivation.
16:
The candle answers the parable before it, and the fathers divide over what is hidden. Bede reads it as the sequel to the privilege just given, that having told the apostles the mysteries were for them and parables for others, the Lord now shows that by them the same mystery must at length be revealed to others. Augustine reads the covering as cowardice rather than reticence, taking the vessel and bed for the flesh and the lamp for the word, so that whoever keeps it hid through fear of the troubles of the flesh sets the flesh before the manifestation of the truth; against that he sets the man who so submits his body to God's service that preaching the truth stands highest and the service of the body lowest. Origen makes the candlestick the whole Church: he who lights the light of reason in his soul must not hide it under a bed where men sleep, since that provides nothing for those entering the house. Chrysostom applies it to the disciples, teaching them to be strong as exposed to the view of all men, fighting in the world as on a stage, since so great virtue cannot lie hid.

What Luke's version adds the two grammarians pick out. Ellicott prefers lamp to candle and lampstand to candlestick, notes the general word vessel where the others have the bushel, and marks the wider range of the light, which reaches not only those in the house but those entering it; he ventures to connect that with the evangelist's own history as a convert from heathenism, who had been among those that entered in and had seen the light the apostles lighted. Robertson notes that another evangelist distributes these sayings over three separate places, and answers the inference: it does not follow that anyone has bunched separate sayings together or scattered a single discourse, since one of the slowest lessons for some critics to learn is that Jesus repeated favourite sayings on different occasions, as every popular preacher does. The proverb about what a man has divides them more sharply. Clarke argues that the common rendering, what he seemeth to have, contradicts itself, since what is possessed in appearance only can be taken away in appearance only, so that there is neither gain nor loss and the text says nothing; from classical usage he shows the verb is often an expletive or an intensive, and concludes it means simply what he hath, these persons having really had the divine seed planted in them. Ellicott and Robertson keep the appearance and make it the point: better, that which he thinks he hath, since the man who does not use his knowledge has no real possession in it.

On the mother and the brethren the fathers are gentler than Calvin expects. Titus takes the word brethren as a doctrine of grace, since no one is the brother of the Saviour in respect of his divine nature, he being the Only-begotten, but he has made us partakers of his flesh and blood and, being God by nature, has become our brother. Chrysostom denies that the answer reproves Mary, holding that it greatly assists her, since he would not have raised her so high if she were always to expect honour from him as a son and never to consider him as her Lord. Theophylact reports a reading in which the message is malicious, brought by men who mocked his teaching and meant to expose his meanness of birth, and answers that low birth harms no one who hears the word of God, though hearing alone saves none and rather condemns. Calvin defends the visitors' motive against two of these fathers by name, allowing that natural affection may have carried them beyond the bounds of propriety but refusing the charge of ambition, since the testimony of the Spirit everywhere commends Mary's piety and modesty.
22:
Why the disciples were put out on the water at all is the first question, and the answers run from the pastoral to the polemical. Cyril says the disciples had seen all men receive help from Christ and it seemed fitting that they too should have the benefit of him, since no one regards another's case as he does his own; so the Lord exposed them to the sea and the winds. Ambrose reads the crossing as the type of every Christian passage: no one can pass from this life without temptations, temptation being the trial of faith, so we are subject to the storms of spiritual wickedness and must awake the Pilot as watchful sailors; and though Christ no longer sleeps in the sleep of his own body, we should beware lest through the sleep of our bodies he be to us asleep. Henry gives the reason from the errand: Christ chose to go by water though he might have gone by land a little way about, that he might show his wonders in the deep; and he guesses that the prince of the power of the air, suspecting Christ was crossing to cast out the legion on the other side, poured out this storm to stop him. Tertullian uses the miracle against an opponent by name, since to ask what manner of man commands the winds and water is not to find a new proprietor of the elements: the rod of Moses waved over a sea ampler than all the lakes of that country, the Jordan stood still at the bidding of Joshua's priests, and the psalm had already said that the Lord is upon many waters.

What this telling adds the two grammarians divide between them, and it is mostly the vocabulary of a physician and a stranger. Ellicott notes that the word for falling asleep differs from the was asleep of the other Gospels and occurs in the New Testament only here, a more technical term and so far characteristic of the physician-historian; that they were filling rather than were filled, the tense describing the process; and that the word rendered Master is one this evangelist alone uses, the more classical of the two, reserving the ordinary word for the Lord's work as a teacher. He observes too that this writer uses the accurate term lake throughout where the other three, written by or under the influence of Galileans, keep the popular sea. Robertson supplies the geography, that these wind storms rushed from the mountain down the gorge upon the small lake and shook it like a tempest, and notes that this is the only passage which speaks of the sleep of Jesus. Clarke works on one English word instead, comparing the phrase for being in jeopardy with the Greek version of the prophet's storm, where the same verb is used of a ship in the utmost danger of being dashed to pieces; and he objects that jeopardy is an inexpressive borrowed term, properly the cry of a disappointed gamester that the game is lost.

On the cry itself Augustine settles a difficulty the others do not raise. The three accounts give three different forms of words, and he says it is not worth while to inquire which was most likely said, since whether they said one of these three or some other of the same import is no matter; and he adds that among the many who awoke him all these things may have been said, one by one and another by another. Ambrose is sharpest on the rebuke that follows: they are rightly reproved who feared while Christ was present, since he who clings to him can in no wise perish. Robertson finds the disciples' uneasiness in the doubled address, and notes that the word for the raging of the water is a boisterous surge rather than the regular swell of the other account.
26:
Where this happened is disputed on the manuscripts. Robertson gives the resolution: the reading here agrees with the second Gospel while the other name belongs to the first, and the discrepancy is cleared up by the discovery of a village of the right name on the steep eastern bank, near the town the other reading points to. Clarke reports three forms without deciding, and Calvin declines a smaller version of the question, whether the man was a citizen or came out of the town to meet Christ, observing that when he was sent home he proclaimed the thing in a neighbouring country, from which it is conjectured he was not a native. On the tombs Calvin refuses three current explanations as idle and foolish — that devils delight in the stench of dead bodies, are gratified by the smell of oblations, or watch over souls desirous to approach their bodies — and gives another: the man was kept among the graves that he might be terrified continually with the mournful spectacle of death, as if cut off from the society of men and already dwelling among the dead. From this he draws his point, that the devil does not only torment men in the present life but pursues them even to death, and that in death his dominion is chiefly exercised.

Augustine reads the scene as a figure of the nations. The brazen fetters signify the harsh laws of the Gentiles, by which offences are restrained in their states; the bursting of them and the driving into the wilderness means that he broke through those laws and was led by lust into crimes beyond the ordinary life of men; the legion signifies the nations that served many devils; and the swine on the mountains are the unclean and proud over whom the evil spirits have dominion because of their idols, men who after the manner of unclean animals have defiled the grace of their natural virtues by the filthy actions of their life. On the request not to be sent into the deep, Clarke supplies a parallel from outside Scripture, that in one school of philosophy certain material demons were said to wander the earth in horror of being sent into abysses, so that if even an old woman threatened them and pronounced the names of the angels whose office that is, their fear would be inexpressible; Robertson gives the word itself, from a privative and the word for deep, used of the deep sea, of the receptacle of the dead, and especially of the abode of demons.

What went into the swine Clarke will not leave alone. Some critics, he says, would have us understand the whole of the man himself, an outrageous maniac who ran after the swine and drove them down the precipice; this is solemn trifling indeed, or at least trifling with solemn things, and it is impossible to read the account as given here and admit that explanation, for on such a plan there is nothing certain in the word of God and every man may give it what meaning he pleases. Titus follows the herdsmen: they fled lest they perish with the swine, and the severity of their loss led them to the Saviour, so that while God punishes men in their substance he blesses their souls; the healed man sat at the feet where he had obtained safety and departed not from them, while the countrymen, who ought to have besought the Lord to stay and guard them, through fear lost their own salvation by asking him to depart. Calvin sets the two responses side by side: how wide is the difference between the knowledge that strikes men with terror and drives them from the presence of God, and the knowledge that draws them gently and makes them feel that nothing is more desirable than to be united to him.
40:
Henry begins from the contrast with the shore just left. Christ was driven away by the Gadarenes, who were weary of him and willing to be rid of him; but when he crossed the water the Galileans gladly received him, having wished and waited for his return, so that if some will not accept the favours he offers, others will, and if one town be not gathered there are many among whom he shall be glorious. He notes too that having finished his work on the far side he came back and found fresh work waiting, since they that lay out themselves to do good shall never want occasion for it. On the ruler's approach he weighs the manner: the address was humble and reverent, for Jairus, though a ruler, fell down at Jesus' feet as owning him a ruler above himself, and importunate, since he besought him to come into his house, not having the faith, or at least not the thought, of the centurion who desired Christ only to speak the word at a distance; and yet Christ complied and went with him.

Why the question who touched me should be asked at all is the difficulty, and the answers are of two kinds. Calvin states the objection plainly, that it does appear absurd that Christ should pour out his grace without knowing on whom he bestowed it, and no easier to suppose the power flowed from him unbidden, as though it were not a free gift given at the times and to the persons he was pleased to select. His answer is that beyond all question he knowingly and willingly cured the woman, and drew her to himself by his Spirit that she might obtain the cure, but put the question to her so that she might freely and publicly make it known; for if Christ had been the only witness of his own miracle his statements might not have been believed, whereas now that the woman, struck with dread, relates what happened to her, greater weight is due to her confession. Gill gives the same reason in a sentence, that he spoke not as ignorant of the person but in order to discover her to the people, and the cure she had received, and her faith along with it. Clarke turns the episode into a rule about faith. The power that went out of him did not proceed always as necessarily as odours do from plants, for then all who touched him must have been equally partakers; of the many that touched him this woman alone received it, because she came in faith, which alone attracts and receives the energetic influence of God at all times. From which he draws the complaint that there would be more miracles, at least of spiritual healing, were there more faith among those who are called believers.

The two grammarians and one historian supply what the others do not. Robertson notes that the words for the crowd's pressure mean to hold thee in and to crush thee, the second used elsewhere of pressing out grapes and occurring in the New Testament only here; and Ellicott observes that the title the disciples use in reply is the distinctive word this evangelist alone employs, the same he had used in the storm. Eusebius alone reports what became of the woman afterwards, that in the city she came from she set up a monument of the mercy shown her: on a lofty pedestal near the entrance to her house stood a brazen statue of a woman on bended knees with her hands joined as if in prayer, and opposite it another figure of the same material, clothed in a stole and holding forth his hand to her, at whose feet a strange plant was growing up to the hem of the brazen robe.
49:
Why the delay had been allowed is Chrysostom's point, and it makes the message from the house part of the design: the Lord conveniently waited until the girl had died, so that the miracle of her raising might be made public, and for that reason he goes slower and speaks longer with the woman, that the ruler's daughter may expire and the messengers come to tell him. Calvin gives the mourners the same evidential weight from the other side, since the evangelists mention the lamentation so that the resurrection may be more fully believed, hired mourners not being present until the death had been ascertained and the funeral preparations were going forward. But he will not let the custom pass without a rebuke: it was the mourners' duty to employ every method for allaying grief, and instead, as though they had not sinned enough in disorderly lamentation, they were eager to heighten it by fresh excitements, which shows how strongly inclined the world is not only to indulge its faults but to promote them. Clarke says the same of the practice in one line, that pompous funeral ceremonies are ridiculous in themselves and entirely opposed to the spirit and simplicity of the religion of Christ. Gill observes only who the company were, not the relations and servants alone but the mourning women hired for the purpose.

Whether the child was really dead the saying about sleep has always been made to raise, and Robertson meets it directly. Some think the remark proves she was not dead but only in a trance; it matters little, he says, since the touch of Christ's hand and the power of his voice restored her to life, and the calling aloud was certainly not to wake the dead but to make it plain to all that she rose in answer to his raised voice. Gill takes the return of her spirit as doctrine, that the soul is immortal and dies not with the body, existing in a separate state after death and hereafter re-entering the body in the resurrection, of which this was a kind of pledge and emblem; where her spirit was during the separation he declines to ask, calling the question needless, and it enough to say that it had returned to God who gave it and was sent back by him. Ellicott notes that this account agrees with the second Gospel in naming the three who were allowed in, where the first omits them.

The command to give her something to eat draws the largest lesson from the smallest detail. Clarke argues that though she was raised by a miracle she was not to be preserved by one, since nature is God's great instrument and he delights to work by it, nor will he do anything by his sovereign power in the way of miracle that can be effected by his ordinary providence; and he presses the parallel, that God will have us be workers together with him, providing food but not eating for us, and providing salvation for a lost world and bestowing it on every penitent believing soul, yet neither repenting nor believing for any man. Ambrose reads the taking of the hand as the figure of a greater feeding, calling him blessed whom wisdom takes by the hand to bring him into her secret places and command that food be given him, since the bread of heaven is the word of God, and it is wisdom who says come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. On the charge of silence that follows, an old Greek expositor finds the proof of the giver's temper, that he shows himself the giver of good things and not covetous of glory, giving the whole and receiving nothing, whereas he who seeks the glory of his works has shown forth something but also receives something.
